tagline: A forested mountain village and spring-fed lakes beyond Las Vegas
intro: State Route 157 provides access to Mount Charleston, a village in the Spring Mountains northwest of Las Vegas. The village lies at approximately 7,500 feet, where rain and snow support coniferous forests. Las Vegas lies at about 2,000 feet; the higher village is a vacation destination for city residents.

Historian Stanley W. Paher places Conrad Keil, also known as Kyle, in the canyon with a sawmill and cabin circa 1870–1880. Edmund W. Griffith established a campground around 1905 and built Charleston Park Lodge around 1915. The Civilian Conservation Corps based Camp Charleston Mountain in the canyon beginning in 1933.

Start with the mountain village, which lies in Kyle Canyon. The Spring Mountains have conifers at their upper elevations, with juniper and pinyon below and creosote bush at their bases. Tule Springs offers a separate Las Vegas excursion to natural spring-fed lakes in the Mojave Desert.

moments.title: Mount Charleston
moments.text: The village’s approximately 7,500-foot elevation puts it above Las Vegas, at about 2,000 feet. Rain and melted snow sustain coniferous forest here. Mount Charleston takes its name from the nearby mountain and occupies a valley known for hiking trails. Its early vacation development included Edmund W. Griffith’s Charleston Park Lodge, later enlarged with a casino and lost to fire in 1961. The lodge stood in what is now Old Town. Historical postcards held by the Pomona, California, public library place that lodge at the present location of the Mount Charleston Library and Volunteer Fire Department.

moments.title: Silent Heroes of the Cold War Memorial
moments.text: A propeller from a downed aircraft forms part of the Silent Heroes of the Cold War Memorial at Spring Mountains Visitor Gateway. Installed in 2015, the memorial recalls a 1955 crash near Mount Charleston’s summit. The aircraft was traveling from Burbank to Groom Lake for work on the secret U-2 program when it crashed during a blizzard. All fourteen men aboard died, including military personnel and civilian contractors, engineers and technicians. The recovered propeller stands with a granite monument; aircraft wreckage also remains near the summit, just off the southern loop trail.

moments.title: Tule Springs
moments.text: Natural spring-fed lakes form a Mojave Desert oasis within Floyd Lamb Park at Tule Springs. The springs also supported a guest ranch for out-of-state residents seeking Nevada divorces. Most ranch buildings date from the 1940s, when Prosper Jacob Goumond developed the divorce ranch. Las Vegas acquired the site as a park in 1964; state control followed in 1977, before the park returned to the city in 2007. Several ranch buildings remain, along with a few peacocks. The ranch became a National Register historic district in 1981. The city operates the park.
